overview.body:
**Odysseús** (*odysseus*) — The Much-Enduring Wanderer · Master of Cunning Return — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Cunning, Journey". The name means "Hated, painful"[^1].

Odysseús is the Greeks' fullest study of intelligence under pressure: the strategist of Troy, the wanderer of ten years, the beggar who comes home to a house full of enemies and wins it back with patience, a bow, and a rooted bed. Homer gives him more words than any other hero — his weapon is speech itself.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Odysseús** and serves its temple at [odysseús.com](https://xn--odysses-c2a.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *odysseus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.
Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Ὀδυσσεύς**. Etymologically it means "Hated, painful"[^1].

The ASCII form *odysseus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Odysseús** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **o** → **O** — O uppercase
- **d** → **d** — d same
- **y** → **y** — y same
- **s** → **s** — s same
- **s** → **s** — s same
- **e** → **e** — e same
- **u** → **ú** — Acute on u
- **s** → **s** — s same

The project holds the domain **odysseús.com** (xn--odysses-c2a.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/o.dys.seús/** — Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **O-** — Short omicron with smooth breathing — the name begins low and unforced.
- **-dys-** — Delta and short upsilon with sigma [dys] — the compact middle the poets linked to ὀδύσσομαι, 'to hate'.
- **-seús** — Sigma plus the diphthong ευ under acute pitch [seús] — the rising, long final syllable of the agentive -εύς names.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'oh-dyss-SEWS' — three quick syllables gathering into a long, high final surge, like a wave cresting at the name's end.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek verb** — ὀδύσσομαι, 'to be wroth with, to hate' — the Odyssey's own etymology: his grandfather Autolykos names him 'the hated one' (Od. 19.407)
- **Homeric epithets** — πολύτροπος 'of many turns', πολύμητις 'of many counsels', πολύτλας 'much-enduring'
- **Western Greek** — dialectal forms with -l- (Ὀλυσσεύς) stand behind the Latin name
- **Latin** — Ulixēs, whence English 'Ulysses'

Odysseús is Tier 1 because the Greek Ὀδυσσεύς contains both stress (the acute on the final syllable) and length (the diphthong ευ). The restoration keeps the acute on ú; the diphthong itself survives in the standard transliteration eu. English 'Odysseus' flattens the pitch that Greek put on the name's last syllable.

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

original-script.body: The name is written in Greek as **Ὀδυσσεύς**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *odysseus* and the PuniCodex restoration **Odysseús** are measured: the restoration preserves its pitch accent of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

domains.body:
Odysseús is the Greeks' fullest study of intelligence under pressure: the strategist of Troy, the wanderer of ten years, the beggar who comes home to a house full of enemies and wins it back with patience, a bow, and a rooted bed. Homer gives him more words than any other hero — his weapon is speech itself.[^1]

### The Strategist

Deviser of the Wooden Horse, and of the name Outis — 'Nobody' — by which he outwitted the Cyclops Polyphêmos.

### The Wayfarer

Ten years from Troy to Ithaka: Cyclops, Kirke, the dead, the Sirens, Skylla and Charybdis, Kalypso — the sea's whole syllabus.

### The Returned King

Disguised as a beggar in his own hall, he strings the great bow and takes back house, wife, and kingdom from the suitors.

### Athena's Favourite

The goddess of counsel delights in him precisely because he is like her: 'among all men you are the best in counsel and speech' (Od. 13).

sources.citation: Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

symbols.body:
The iconography associated with Odysseús concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The great bow** — The weapon only he could string; the test by which the beggar becomes the king
- **The olive-trunk bed** — Built into a living, rooted tree — the immovable sign by which Penelope knows her husband
- **The scar** — The boar's-tusk wound from Parnassos, by which the old nurse Eurykleia knows him first
- **The oar** — Carried inland until a wayfarer mistakes it for a winnowing-fan — the prophecy of his peace
- **The ship** — The vessel of the much-turned man; he loses every one and still comes home

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

mythology.body:
The Odyssey is his biography, but his story begins in the Iliad and ends in prophecy. He is the one hero whose full arc — war, wandering, homecoming — the tradition preserves entire.[^1]

### The Wooden Horse (The Ruse)

Ten years of force had not taken Troy; Odysseús took it in a night by craft. The horse, built by Epeios with Athena's help, carried the pick of the Achaeans within the walls as a pretended offering, and the Odyssey remembers it as his design. The Iliad ends before the fall, but the Odyssey tells the rest: the plan, the peril of Helen's voice at the horse's side, and the sack that followed were all his.[^2]

### Nobody and the Enchantress (The Wandering)

Blown off course, he meets the story-book of the sea: the Lotus-Eaters; Polyphêmos, outwitted by the name Outis — 'Nobody' — and blinded as he sleeps; Aiolos's bag of winds; the Laistrygonians; Kirke, who turns his crew to swine and then becomes his teacher; the descent to the dead, where Teiresias foretells the road home; the Sirens heard from the mast; Skylla and Charybdis; and Thrinakia, where his last crew eats the Sun's cattle and is lost.

### Kalypso and the Raft (The Wrath of the Sea)

For the blinding of his son Polyphêmos, Poseidôn pursues him. Seven years he is kept on Kalypso's island, offered immortality and a goddess's bed — and refuses both for a sight of the smoke of Ithaka. Released by Zeús's command, he builds a raft, is wrecked by the sea-god within sight of Scheria, and comes ashore naked on the Phaiakians' mercy — the low point from which everything turns.

### The Bow and the Rooted Bed (The Return)

Landed on Ithaka at last, he enters his hall disguised as a beggar and endures the suitors' insults in silence. Penelope sets the contest of the bow; he alone strings it, and the hall runs with the suitors' blood. Even then she tests him, bidding the bed be moved — and he cries out that it cannot be, for he built it round a rooted olive. Teiresias's prophecy remains: a last journey inland with an oar, until the sea is unknown, and a gentle death in old age.

sources.citation: Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.
Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

syncretism.body:
The western Greeks pronounced his name with -l-, and through them it reached Italy: Latin Ulixēs, English Ulysses. Rome admired his cunning and distrusted it; Virgil's Aeneid makes him the face of Greek deceit, while the philosophers reclaimed him as the Stoic sage. Dante's Ulisse sails beyond the Pillars of Herakles and drowns for the love of knowledge — the Christian epic's answer to Homer. Long before all this, the Odyssey itself had performed the boldest syncretism: it turned a folktale wanderer into the type of every human journey, so that his name, as the common noun 'odyssey', no longer needs him at all.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

cultural-legacy.body: He is the most rewritten figure of the ancient world: Sophocles' divided portraits, Euripides' stage villain, Tennyson's aging voyager ('to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield'), Joyce's Ulysses, in which a Dublin advertisement canvasser lives the whole epic in a day, Kazantzakis's modern sequel, Cavafy's Ithaka — 'wise as you will have become, so full of experience' — and a hundred films and novels. Space probes and wanderers' memoirs borrow the noun he became. Restoring Odysseús keeps the stress Greek put on his last syllable: the name itself rises at the end, like a mast coming over the horizon.[^1]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

archaeology.body: Ithaki, the island that still bears his name, has Mycenaean remains at Pelikata and Aetos, and at Polis Bay a cave sanctuary of the Nymphs whose votive deposits run from the Late Bronze Age to the Roman period — the very cave where later Ithacans placed Odysseús's homecoming, and where a Hellenistic terracotta fragment inscribed ΕΥΧΗΝ ΟΔΥΣΣΕΙ, 'a prayer to Odysseus', attests his hero-cult. The Bronze Age site above Polis Bay, long called the School of Homer, remains conjectural as his palace. Beyond Ithaka his cult is epigraphic and scattered; his truest monument is Homer's text.[^1]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

homeric-hymns.body: Odysseús has no hymn — the corpus hymns gods, and he is the most mortal of heroes — but three hymns address the powers between whom his life was wagered. The Hymn to Athena celebrates the goddess of counsel who delights in him precisely because he is like her, 'best of men in counsel and speech'; the great birth-hymn to Athena, of the goddess springing armed from the head of Zeús, hymns the craft he personifies among men.[^1] The Hymn to Hermês hymns the other cunning mind of his story, the god who hands him the moly against Kirke's pharmaka.[^2] And the short Hymn to Poseidôn addresses the 'mover of the earth' whose anger is the Odyssey's engine.[^3] The pattern is exact: the man receives no hymn because the poems had already made him the battleground of the hymned. His genre was the epic itself — the one hero whose patron, guide, and persecutor all have hymns of their own.

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 13.296–299; Homeric Hymn 28, to Athena.
Homer, Odyssey 10.275–306 (the moly); Homeric Hymn 4, to Hermês.
Homeric Hymn 22, to Poseidôn.

epithets.body:
- **πολύτροπος** (polýtropos) — 'of many turns' — the Odyssey's first word for him (Od. 1.1): turned by travel, by guile, by reversal.[^1]
- **πολύμητις** (polýmētis) — 'of many counsels' — the standing formula of the Iliad; wisdom as his defining excellence.[^1]
- **πολύτλας** (polýtlas) — 'much-enduring' — paired with δῖος, 'godlike', in the Odyssey's recurrent line 'much-enduring godlike Odysseús'.[^1]
- **πολυμήχανος** (polymḗchanos) — 'of many devices' — the resourcefulness Helen recalls on the walls of Troy.[^1]
- **πτολίπορθος** (ptolíporthos) — 'sacker of cities' — the warrior's formula that ties his name to Troy's fall.[^1]
- **Λαερτιάδης** (Laertiádēs) — 'son of Laertes' — the patronymic under which he both hides and reveals himself; his lying tales make it the poem's ironic touchstone.[^1]

No Greek hero carries so many epithets, because no Greek hero is so many men: the formulas measure, one by one, the turns of the man of many turns.[^2]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad and Odyssey (the formulaic epithets of Odysseús).
Liddell-Scott-Jones and Beekes, s.v. Ὀδυσσεύς.

oracle-sites.body: The Odyssey gives its hero one consultation and one homecoming shrine, and archaeology has made the second real. The consultation is the strangest in Greek literature: no living oracle, but the dead themselves — Odysseús sails to the world's edge and pours blood for the shades until Teiresias rises and reads him his road home and his death 'from the sea'.[^1] The shrine is the Cave of the Nymphs on Ithaki, which Homer describes with a precision that reads like a survey — stone bowls and amphorae, bees, looms of stone, and two entrances, one for mortals and one for gods (Od. 13.102–112).[^2] At Polis Bay on Ithaki a cave answering that description received votives from the Late Bronze Age to the Roman period — tripods that later visitors associated with the Phaiakian treasure hidden there at Athena's counsel, and a Hellenistic terracotta fragment inscribed ΕΥΧΗΝ ΟΔΥΣΣΕΙ, 'a prayer to Odysseus': the written receipt of his hero-cult.[^3] Beyond Ithaki his cult remained epigraphic and scattered; he never received a civic oracle. His sacred geography is exactly his story's — one ghost consulted at the edge of the world, one cave where the wanderer was finally home.

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 11 (the consultation of Teiresias).
Homer, Odyssey 13.102–112.
The Polis cave votive deposit, Ithaki (British School at Athens excavations); the ΕΥΧΗΝ ΟΔΥΣΣΕΙ inscription.

iconography.body: Ancient viewers could spot Odysseús by a single attribute: the píleos, the round felt sailor's cap that is his signature from archaic art onward — the traveler's hat of the man who is always arriving by sea.[^1] The great vase subjects are the Odyssey's own set pieces: the blinding of Polyphêmos, the crew escaping beneath the rams; the Sirens' island, with the hero bound to the mast as the ship sails past — the subject of the famous Attic stamnos in the British Museum; Kirke with her cup and wand; and the return: the beggar with staff and wallet, the scar revealed at the washing of feet, the bow drawn in the hall.[^2] Roman art extended the cycle on sarcophagi and wall paintings, where the Sirens and the recognition before [[penelope|Pēnelopē]] remained favorites.[^3] Unlike the gods, he has no animal and no weapon of his own: his iconography is biographical, a portrait of situations — the one hero ancient art identifies not by what he carries but by what he is enduring.

sources.citation: The Attic and Roman figural tradition (the píleos as Odysseús's attribute); British Museum, the 'Siren Vase' stamnos.
Homer, Odyssey 9, 12, 19–22 (the painted episodes).
Apollodorus, Epitome 7 (the return cycle in later tradition).

meditation.body:
Every other hero of the Trojan cycle is defined by what he can overpower; Odysseús is defined by what he can outlast. The epic tests him with each kind of loss — companions, ships, time, fame, even identity: he survives the Cyclops precisely by becoming Nobody, and he survives Kalypso precisely by refusing to become a god. Between those two refusals lies his whole philosophy. A man is not his name, and yet the name is all that comes home.

The ending refuses triumph. The suitors are dead, the hall is his, and still the wife he won must test him, and the test is not valor but knowledge: only the true husband knows the bed cannot move because it was built on a living root. That rootedness is the answer to all the wandering — the one unmoving thing in a life of motion, grown not made. And beyond even that, Teiresias's oar waits: the promise that he must carry the sea inland until it is no longer recognized. The man of many turns earns his peace only where nobody knows what an oar is — where even his story cannot follow him.[^1]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.
